title: Asian stocks edge higher as Fed decision looms, oil rally pauses
full_text:
U.S. stocks end in the red a day ahead of Fed rate decision as yields, oil surge
Investing.com -- Asian stocks edged higher on Wednesday as investors awaited the Federal Reserve's interest-rate decision, with gains in South Korea and Japan helping the region recover from recent losses.
The MSCI Asia Pacific index rose about 0.2%, while South Korea’sKOSPI gained 0.9% and Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 0.6%. Hong Kong’s {Hang Seng slipped 0.2%.
U.S. equity futures were also modestly higher, with Nasdaq 100 Futures andS&P 500 Futures gaining 0.2%, each. Markets are pricing a 92.4% probability of a 25-basis-point Fed hike on Wednesday, up sharply from 59.4% a week earlier, which would mark the first increase since 2023.
The Bank of England follows Thursday and the Bank of Japan on Friday, making this a pivotal stretch for global monetary policy.
Bond markets have been under pressure ahead of the decision. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield briefly topped 5% on Tuesday, its highest since 2007, before easing to around 4.99% in Asian trade. The move reflected weaker Treasury buybacks and concerns over fiscal deficits, heavy debt issuance and AI-related financing needs.
Chip stocks rebound as AI debate shifts toward economics
Asian technology shares were mixed. SK Hynix rose 2.3% and Samsung Electronics gained 1.5%, while Kioxia fell 4%. Murata Manufacturing gained 1.6%, Largan rose 4.6%, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing slipped 0.2%.
OCBC Head of Wealth Advisory Chez Anbu said markets remain resilient but could trade sideways until there is greater clarity on Fed policy, inflation and September seasonality.
OCBC remains constructive on equities while advocating diversification, lower-volatility and income-generating assets, selective participation in the long-term AI theme and broader exposure across the technology value chain.
Oil offered some relief, with Brent down about 0.6% around $108 a barrel after a roughly 20% gain this month.
Supply concerns remain tied to the war involving Iran and disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz, while Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline remains affected by attacks. U.S. crude inventories also rose unexpectedly, helping temper the rally.
China data highlight uneven recovery; Indonesia gets policy boost
Mainland China’s CSI 300 rose 0.6% and the Shanghai Composite gained 0.5%. August industrial output rose 5.2%, but retail sales grew just 0.4%, while fixed-asset investment fell 7.2% in the first eight months and property investment dropped 19.9%, highlighting weak domestic demand despite resilient factory activity.
Hong Kong technology shares were mixed, with Alibaba falling 0.5%, Meituan 1.3%, JD.com 1.22% and Tencent 1%, while MiniMax jumped 5.2% and Z.AI gained 6%.
Maybank analysts said the AI slowdown debate reflects concerns over monetization as model prices fall and capex rises, rather than a halt in spending. For Hong Kong and China, they favor chip and infrastructure beneficiaries of cheaper open-weight AI, while pure-model and capex-heavy platforms face greater scrutiny.
Meanwhile, data showed Japan’s August exports rose 19.3%, while imports jumped 28%, leaving a ¥1.106 trillion trade deficit; exports to the U.S. and China rose 24.9% and 20.6%, respectively.
Indonesia’s Jakarta Composite rose 0.7% after President Prabowo Subianto appointed Suahasil Nazara as finance minister. Maybank analysts said his appointment could reduce risk premia and benefit large banks and rate-sensitive sectors including property, cement and towers.
Elsewhere, Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.3%, New Zealand’s NZX 50 rose 0.8%, Singapore’s Straits Times added 0.2%, while India’s Nifty 50 futures rose 0.4%.

Investing.com -- NVIDIA Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang is expected to attend a state dinner hosted by U.S. President Donald Trump for Chinese President Xi Jinping next week, according to multiple media reports on Tuesday.
The reports, citing people familiar with the matter, said Huang is expected to join the dinner when Xi visits Washington for talks with Trump on September 24.
Huang's presence would put a leading U.S. artificial-intelligence executive at a high-profile diplomatic event as Washington and Beijing prepare for talks spanning economic and technology issues.
AI is expected to be among the topics discussed when Trump and Xi meet, CNBC reported.
The appearance would also come as Nvidia remains at the center of debates over AI's rapid development and U.S.-China technology competition.
Nvidia is a major supplier of chips used by AI developers, while the United States and China remain the two leading forces in the development and deployment of advanced AI systems.
Huang has maintained close ties with Trump and was among a select group of U.S. business leaders who traveled to China with the president earlier this year.
He also attended a state dinner hosted by Xi for Trump during the U.S. president's visit to China in May, alongside Elon Musk and former Apple CEO Tim Cook.
The White House did not immediately comment on Huang's reported attendance, according to CNBC and Reuters.

title: Meta’s Zuckerberg supports AI safety evaluators over development slowdown
full_text:
U.S. stocks end in the red a day ahead of Fed rate decision as yields, oil surge
Investing.com-- Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg on Tuesday evening said artificial intelligence developers should rely on independent safety evaluators for their models, instead of slowing development.
Zuckerberg said in an X post that AI labs that don’t focus on “alignment” with users will fall behind, and that developers should engage independent evaluators and advisers.
“There is a lot of debate about slowing progress on capabilities until alignment catches up. My view is that trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models,” Zuckerberg said.

He said Meta had delayed shipping its latest Muse AI model to focus on safety and security.
“Engaging independent evaluators and advisors is industry best practice… it would be helpful for there to be a larger and more diverse ecosystem of evaluators,” Zuckerberg said in a statement.
The Meta CEO’s comments come amid a growing debate over AI safety, especially after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay calling for a slowdown in AI development due to the potential threats posed by the fast-growing technology.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, xAI CEO Elon Musk, and several other major AI executives endorsed Amodei’s message. But others, chiefly Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, dismissed concerns over safety– a message that was also pushed by President Donald Trump.
Zuckerberg’s comments on Wednesday were more in line with a stance espoused by Nvidia’s Huang, who slammed proposals for AI companies to receive antitrust exemptions to coordinate a slowdown in development.
Huang said AI developers should be able to solve safety issues by themselves, and that model makers should also take more responsibility for their creations.

title: Oil prices dip as U.S. inventory build offsets M.East supply jitters
full_text:
U.S. stocks end in the red a day ahead of Fed rate decision as yields, oil surge
Investing.com-- Oil prices fell on Wednesday as data pointing to an unexpected build in U.S. inventories overshadowed continued supply disruptions in the Middle East after Saudi Arabia halted loadings at a major port due to Houthi attacks.
Crude was also subject to some profit-taking after appreciating sharply in recent weeks on worsening Houthi-Saudi hostilities and a continued standoff in the Strait of Hormuz.
Brent oil futures fell 0.5% to $108.22 a barrel by 21:05 ET (01:05 GMT), while West Texas Intermediate crude futures fell 0.8% to $105.0 a barrel.
Traders were wary of any big bets ahead of a closely watched Federal Reserve meeting later in the day, where the central bank is widely expected to hike interest rates.
Get more insights on oil markets and the M.East war with InvestingPro-- with 55% for a limited time
API data shows unexpected build in U.S. inventories
Data from the American Petroleum Institute showed U.S. inventories unexpectedly grew 7.14 million barrels in the week to September 11, more than expectations for a 1.8 mb draw.
The print usually heralds a similar reading from official inventory data, which is due later on Wednesday.
But the API data indicated that despite global supply disruptions, stockpiles in the world’s largest fuel consumer remained steady.
Still, the build could also stem from continued releases from the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Data from the Energy Information Administration showed the SPR shrank by nearly 130 mb so far in 2026, to 285.36 million barrels.
M.East supply disruptions persist
Bigger losses in oil were largely limited by continued supply disruptions in the Middle East.
Reports showed that Saudi Arabia had halted loading at its Yanbu port after the world’s biggest crude exporter shut its East-West pipeline amid attacks from Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis in recent weeks.
The Houthis were seen launching more strikes on Saudi Arabia this week, with Riyadh stating early-Wednesday it had intercepted a drone south of the Holy City of Mecca.
The Houthis had earlier this month secured key positions along the Red Sea, allowing them to strike tankers in the Bab el-Mandeb strait and further disrupt oil supplies in the region. Houthi aggression against the Saudis is expected to disrupt about 4% to 5% of global oil supplies.
This came against the backdrop of a continued U.S.-Iran standoff in the Strait of Hormuz, which kept oil flows through the key waterway at a fraction of prewar levels.
Brent was trading up nearly 4% this week after adding 8% apiece in the last two weeks, as markets priced for more supply disruptions.

title: Reliance Worldwide shares hit 1-year high on Brookfield’s $2.9 bln takeover
full_text:
U.S. stocks end in the red a day ahead of Fed rate decision as yields, oil surge
Investing.com -- Reliance Worldwide Corp (ASX:RWC) shares hit an over one-year high on Wednesday after Brookfield agreed to acquire the Australian plumbing-products maker in a deal valuing the company at about A$4.1 billion ($2.9 billion) including debt.
Shares rose 6.5% to A$4.61, their highest since August 18, 2025, while the S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.3%.
Brookfield will pay A$4.75 a share in cash, valuing Reliance Worldwide at about A$4.1 billion on an enterprise-value basis.
The offer represents a substantial premium to the company’s pre-bid trading levels and follows earlier approaches of A$4.15, A$4.25 and A$4.50 a share.
Reliance Worldwide’s directors have unanimously endorsed the deal. Shareholders will have the option to receive the consideration in either Australian or U.S. dollars.
The agreement follows a period of difficult trading for Reliance Worldwide. The company reported FY26 revenue of US$1.31 billion, down 0.7%, while adjusted EBITDA fell 12.8% to US$242.1 million, amid U.S. tariffs, higher copper costs, weaker end markets and cost inflation. Adjusted net profit fell 15.3% to US$125.1 million.
Brookfield’s proposal emerged after four approaches this year, with the latest A$4.75 offer submitted in early August following an approximately eight-week due-diligence process. Reliance Worldwide had granted Brookfield exclusivity through September 15 while the two companies worked toward a binding deal.
The transaction also comes with a 30-day go-shop provision, allowing Reliance Worldwide to solicit and negotiate alternative proposals after signing the scheme implementation deed. That provision had been agreed as part of the earlier process deed.
Brookfield has highlighted Reliance Worldwide’s international plumbing-products business and its exposure to the U.S. market as part of the investment case. Reliance Worldwide owns brands including SharkBite, Cash Acme and John Guest and has operations across North America, Australia, Europe and other markets.
The company had also been restructuring its manufacturing footprint, including the planned closure of brass casting, forging and machining operations in Melbourne.

title: Gold slips ahead of Fed decision as oil, yields keep rate-hike bets elevated
full_text:
U.S. stocks end in the red a day ahead of Fed rate decision as yields, oil surge
Investing.com -- Gold prices edged lower on Wednesday as elevated oil prices and a renewed rise in Treasury yields kept pressure on bullion ahead of the Federal Reserve’s policy decision later in the day.
Markets are pricing a roughly 92% chance of a rate hike, while investors also weigh the risk that stubborn inflation could keep longer-term borrowing costs elevated.
At 21:57 ET (01:57 GMT), XAU/USD fell 0.3% to $4,281.93 an ounce, while Gold Futures declined 0.3% to $4,321.26. XAG/USD slipped 0.2% to $63.57 an ounce, while XPT/USD fell 0.5% to $1,770.33. The US Dollar Index rose marginally by 0.1% to 99.73.
Oil, bond yields strengthen Fed hike expectations
Gold has fallen for two sessions and is now down more than 3% in September, after trading above $4,700 an ounce in late August as traders repeatedly recalibrated the outlook for monetary policy.
The latest pressure comes as high oil prices continue to reinforce inflation concerns. Oil steadied after rising for two straight sessions, while uncertainty over the duration of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline shutdown kept energy markets on edge.
The pipeline was attacked last week and had been carrying millions of barrels of oil a day around the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia has not said how long the shutdown will last or how quickly it can increase shipments through Hormuz to compensate.
Saudi Aramco has also delayed some deliveries to European customers, adding to concerns over available supply.
Those energy risks are feeding into the bond market. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield briefly reached 5.04%, its highest level since 2007, after rising as much as five basis points on Tuesday.
The move is part of a broader global bond selloff driven by booming capital investment and surging energy prices, both of which are adding to inflation pressures.
The 10-year Treasury yield is a key benchmark for borrowing costs globally. Higher yields also weigh on gold because bullion pays no interest, making income-generating assets more attractive.
Fed decision, technical levels set next test
Markets are now pricing roughly a 92% probability of a Fed rate hike, with traders expecting the central bank to raise rates for the first time since 2023.
A hike is not the only risk for bonds and gold. Should the Fed leave rates unchanged or Chair Kevin Warsh sound noncommittal on further increases, investors could demand even higher yields on longer-dated Treasuries to protect against the risk that inflation remains elevated.
Tony Sycamore, senior market analyst at IG, said gold finished marginally lower overnight at around $4,293, pressured by higher energy prices, rising bond yields, a stronger dollar and risk-aversion flows ahead of the Fed decision.
Sycamore said gold needs to reclaim its 200-day moving average near $4,539 to signal that the pullback from the $4,697 high is complete and the broader uptrend has resumed. Until that happens, he sees scope for a deeper decline toward support near $4,200.
Despite the recent weakness, gold remains well above the roughly $4,000 floor seen in July, while many investors continue to expect the metal to regain momentum as its longer-term portfolio-hedging appeal returns.

title: Chinese investors rush into US stocks as Beijing opens wider path overseas
full_text:
U.S. stocks end in the red a day ahead of Fed rate decision as yields, oil surge
SHANGHAI, Sept 16 (Reuters) - Chinese investors are piling into foreign assets, especially U.S. stock funds, after regulators lifted outbound quotas, unlocking pent-up demand as domestic yields are at rock bottom and Beijing tightens unofficial routes for moving money abroad.
While China has cracked down on what it deems illegal overseas investing through online brokerages, it has simultaneously broadened authorised channels to foreign markets.
Late last month China’s foreign exchange regulator raised the outstanding Qualified Domestic Institutional Investor quota by $6.8 billion to a record $183 billion. The speed with which U.S.-focused funds moved to curb inflows just days later underscores investors’ scramble for exposure to Wall Street.
The daily inflow cap on a QDII fund tracking the Nasdaq 100 was raised from 10 yuan to 5,000 yuan on September 9. Just a day later, its fund manager Wanjia Asset Management sharply limited inflows again to 100 yuan daily for an individual investor.
"It means there was explosive inflows so the fund manager needed to limit the subscriptions," said Ivan Shi, head of research at fund consultancy Z-Ben Advisors. "There remains huge appetite in China for U.S. tech stocks."
The rush overseas highlights Beijing’s growing challenge in stemming capital outflows. Confidence in the domestic economy remains fragile, China’s 10-year government bond yield sits more than three percentage points below U.S. Treasury yields, and the local stock market has broadly lagged the double-digit gains delivered by U.S. equities this year.
Portfolio investment hit a record $426 billion deficit in 2025, according to China’s Balance of Payments data, and net outflows reached $146 billion in the first quarter of this year.
In another case, China Universal Asset Management eased restrictions on its Nasdaq 100 ETF, only to tighten curbs again two days later. TruValue Asset Management took a similar U-turn on its QDII fund investing in global chip stocks.
"Chinese demand for global asset allocation is getting bigger and bigger," said Xu Jie, fund manager at Yuanzi Investment Management, which invests in global markets through exchange-traded funds (ETFs) under QDII.
Long-term investors need to "diversify risks and share growth in major global markets."
The U.S. is the top destination for QDII funds, accounting for nearly half of the roughly 1 trillion yuan ($150 billion) business, according to Shanghai Securities.
Most U.S.-bound ETFs trade at a hefty premium to their net asset value, reflecting investors’ eagerness to secure limited overseas exposure. A Shenzhen-listed ETF tracking the Nasdaq-100 Technology Sector Index traded at a premium of 24% on Wednesday.
"The premium just reflects strong household demand on global assets," said Zhaopeng Xing, senior China strategist at ANZ.
China’s balance of payments turned positive recently due to strong trade inflows, "but the regulators still need a balance to control outflows," he said.
($1 = 6.7131 Chinese yuan renminbi)

title: Factbox-How AI leaders and world governments react to ’AI doom’ fears
full_text:
U.S. stocks end in the red a day ahead of Fed rate decision as yields, oil surge
Sept 15 (Reuters) - Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slowdown in the pace of advanced AI development on Saturday, winning rare backing from SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and sparking a debate over AI "doomerism".
Here is what some AI leaders and world governments said about risks associated with AI:
DARIO AMODEI, CEO OF ANTHROPIC
In an essay titled "We Must Pace the Frontier", Amodei said AI progress has accelerated "drastically faster" since summer 2026, driven primarily by AI’s growing ability to build the next generation of AI.
He cited the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident, where an AI "swarm" conducted cybersecurity attacks, as a pivotal event demonstrating AI’s potential for "catastrophic damage" if capabilities grow without guardrails.
Amodei proposed a three-step plan for pacing AI development, including stronger safety testing and independent evaluations of advanced models, coordination among leading AI companies and international cooperation.
SAM ALTMAN, CEO OF OPENAI
"I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier. This has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had at OpenAI in recent weeks," Altman said as he reposted Amodei’s post on X.
He said OpenAI intends to adopt the idea proposed by Anthropic by committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access.
Altman had warned about the risks well before the current AI boom. In a 2015 essay titled "Machine Intelligence, part 1", he said the "development of superhuman machine intelligence is probably the greatest threat to the continued existence of humanity."
ELON MUSK, CEO OF SPACEX
"Dario is right," the billionaire entrepreneur said on X, responding to Amodei’s post.
Musk was among backers of a 2023 push by the non-profit Future of Life Institute to halt AI development for six months to allow time for safety guardrails.
He was also among a group of AI and robotics researchers who wrote an open letter in 2015 that advocated a global ban on "offensive autonomous weapons".
BILL GATES, CO-FOUNDER OF MICROSOFT
"No government in the world is ready for the changes artificial intelligence will bring to society," Gates told Reuters.
The billionaire philanthropist had been optimistic about AI’s health applications, but has recently warned of threats to jobs, concerns about attacks and the dangers of addiction to AI companions, and called for an international organization to manage the technology.
Gates’ namesake foundation plans to spend at least $1 billion in the next two years on expanding people’s access to AI.
DEMIS HASSABIS, CHIEF SCIENTIST AT ALPHABET
"Dario’s essay points towards the right path forward," the former CEO of Google DeepMind said in a response to Amodei’s X post, adding the details needed to be worked through.
Google announced last month that Hassabis, a Nobel Prize recipient, would take the newly created title of Alphabet’s chief scientist and transition from DeepMind CEO to its chairman.
ANDREJ KARPATHY, OPENAI CO-FOUNDER, NOW AT ANTHROPIC
"I love this and really hope we can come together as an industry and make it happen," the founding member of OpenAI said on X while sharing a screenshot of Amodei’s essay.
Karpathy, a highly influential member in the AI community, played a key role in developing Tesla’s self-driving and AI technology before leaving the company in 2022. He joined Anthropic in May.
UNITED STATES
"The only control or ’guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that China would benefit from doubt being cast on AI development.
A Senate aide and a lobbyist familiar with the matter said Senate negotiators were debating legislation that would require AI companies to demonstrate they are taking reasonable precautions to keep their tools from causing harm.
CHINA
State-backed Global Times said in an editorial that the true agenda of Amodei’s essay was "to attempt to curb China’s AI development through technological barriers and regulatory monopolies, uphold Washington’s monopolistic hegemony in cutting-edge technology, and exclude China from the global AI governance system."
China’s state security minister, Chen Yixin, wrote in a government outlet that advanced U.S. models such as Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI’s GPT-5.5-Cyber could pose serious risks to China’s critical information infrastructure, and called for a comprehensive strengthening of AI security.
EUROPEAN UNION
"The European Union is in favour of developing innovation in artificial intelligence, but companies have to prove their services are safe for citizens to operate in the bloc," European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said.
European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde warned the EU was facing an unprecedented risk of being cut off from AI, saying Europe needed to become a producer of AI technology to preserve its autonomy.
GERMANY
"We do not consider halting (AI) development to be a viable option for Europe," Germany’s digital affairs ministry said, adding that strengthening Europe’s digital sovereignty required further AI development and innovation.
Berlin said it was monitoring global AI developments very closely and took public warnings from leading developers seriously.
SPAIN
Digital Transformation Minister Oscar Lopez said there was growing discussion about the need for an international agreement to manage AI risks, likening some proposals to nuclear non-proliferation agreements.

title: European stocks rise from 3-month lows as traders await high-stakes Fed decision
full_text:
U.S. stocks end in the red a day ahead of Fed rate decision as yields, oil surge
Investing.com - European equities edged marginally higher on Wednesday, stabilizing after a severe sell-off pushed continental bourses to multi-month lows, as market participants hesitated to place heavy directional bets ahead of the Federal Reserve’s high-stakes interest rate decision.
The Stoxx Europe 600 Index rose 0.5%, managing a tentative rebound after sliding to its lowest level in three months during Tuesday’s session. The modest advance reflects a tactical breather across regional bourses, which have been heavily battered by triple-digit crude oil prices, escalating Middle East maritime risks, and elevated risk-free yields.
Germany’s DAX gained and London’s FTSE 100 gained 0.4%, while France’s CAC 40 rose 0.3%. Spain’s IBEX 35 and Italy’s FTSE MIB rose 0.6%.
All eyes on Fed decision
Global equity and fixed-income bourses are effectively locked in a holding pattern as the Federal Open Market Committee concludes its two-day policy meeting later in the day.
Interest rate futures monitored via CME FedWatch now price in roughly a 92% probability of a 25-basis-point interest rate increase.
That represents a dramatic repricing from just a week ago when market odds favored a coin flip, driven higher by sticky U.S. inflation data and Brent crude holding firm past $113 a barrel following Saudi pipeline attacks and Red Sea shipping bottlenecks.
A quarter-point move would mark the Federal Reserve’s first rate hike since mid-2023, following the European Central Bank’s decision last week to raise its benchmark deposit facility rate to 2.50%.
Warsh guidance takes center stage
With a 25-basis-point rate increase almost fully discounted by asset markets, trading desks are focusing intensely on Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh’s post-meeting press conference and updated policy projections.
Institutional allocators are looking for clarity on whether Warsh frames this move as a standalone, insurance recalibration against energy volatility or the opening salvo of a barrage of rate hikes to tame second-round inflation.
The central bank decision arrives alongside compounding global rate pressures. The Bank of Japan is widely expected to lift borrowing costs by 25 basis points to 1.25% on Friday, while the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield lingers near multi-year peaks after briefly breaching the 5% threshold on Tuesday.

title: U.S. 10-yr Treasury yields cool below 5% as Fed rate decision approaches
full_text:
U.S. stocks end in the red a day ahead of Fed rate decision as yields, oil surge
Investing.com-- Benchmark U.S. Treasury yields fell below 5% early Wednesday after crossing levels last seen in 2007 earlier this week, with focus squarely on a potential interest rate hike by the Federal Reserve this week.
The 10-year Treasury yield fell slightly to 4.994% by 00:57 ET (04:57 GMT), after rallying as high as 5.03% on Tuesday.
Yields had surged this week as markets priced in a greater chance the Fed will raise rates by 25 basis points at the conclusion of a two-day meeting on Wednesday. The hike will put rates at a one-year high.
Markets are pricing in a 89.5% chance the Fed will hike rates on Wednesday, CME Fedwatch showed.
Sticky inflation prints, soaring oil prices, and hawkish warnings from several Fed policymakers saw markets largely preparing for a hike this week.
But the spike in yields lost some steam on Tuesday after soft New York manufacturing data spurred some concerns over the long-term outlook for the economy.
Investors also bought back into bond markets after extended selling in recent weeks.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended the Donald Trump administration’s economic policies before Congress on Tuesday. Bessent said rising bond yields were due to “global issues,” but acknowledged that Washington needed to address its ballooning fiscal deficit.
Bessent also defended the Treasury’s measures to quash yields, chiefly its doubling of longer-term debt buybacks.
But yields had largely risen past Bessent’s recent measures, with markets now watching to see whether the 10-year rate’s foray beyond 5% would attract more measures from the Treasury.

title: Tonnellerie Francois Freres shares fall 7% on Q1 revenue drop, U.S. destocking
full_text:
U.S. stocks end in the red a day ahead of Fed rate decision as yields, oil surge
Investing.com -- Shares of Tonnellerie Francois Freres fell as much as 7.7% before paring losses to trade 2.1% lower at €15.72 on Wednesday, after the French oak barrel maker reported first-quarter revenue fell 36.4% to €56.9 million due to customer destocking in the United States and a slowdown in bourbon demand.
The bourbon division posted a sharper-than-expected 46% decline at the start of the fiscal year, as extended distillery closures slowed the pace of deliveries during the quarter, TFF said.
Revenue in the alcohol division fell 41.2% to €21.9 million, while wine division revenue dropped 32.9% to €35 million on weak U.S. demand, hurt by a low dollar and persistently high inventory levels.
TFF said its full-year activity forecasts are also affected by a decline in European wine harvest volumes in 2026 following extreme heat and drought over the summer.

title: EU will use all tools to cut China trade deficit, von der Leyen says
full_text:
U.S. stocks end in the red a day ahead of Fed rate decision as yields, oil surge
BRUSSELS, Sept 16 (Reuters) - The European Union will use every possible means to reduce its "unsustainable" trade deficit trade with China, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Wednesday.
Von der Leyen said that the imbalance, with a goods trade deficit of €1 billion ($1.15 billion) a day last year, had reached a tipping point and that Europe was already suffering from the second China shock through deindustrialisation.
EU leaders called on the European Commission in June to produce results from dialogue with China and to ensure the bloc has all the instruments it needed to defend its interests. European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic, leading the talks, said he wanted to achieve tangible results by October.
Von der Leyen said in her ’state of the Union’ address to the European Parliament that it was in both sides’ interests to work together to find a solution.
"Let me be clear: we will use all the tools at our disposal to rebalance our relationship. Words are good. But deeds are better," she said.
Von der Leyen also highlighted the EU’s reliance on China for many critical minerals, notably rare earths.
"We need to urgently procure and build up our reserves," she said, adding the EU would establish a new European Corporation on critical raw materials to help the 27-nation bloc obtain and stockpile what it needed.

The U.S. dollar index was around 99.59, little changed, while the USD/JPY pair slipped marginally to 154.97 after the yen fell to a one-week low of 155.49 earlier in the session. The EUR/USD pair rose 0.07% to 1.15, while the GBP/USD pair was around 1.35.
The Bank of England will announce its policy decision on Thursday, with markets currently leaning toward a hold despite a renewed rise in U.K. inflation.
August consumer-price inflation accelerated to 3.1% from 2.9% in July, while core inflation held at 2.6% and services inflation remained at 3.4%. Markets were pricing roughly a one-in-three chance of a 25-basis-point hike this week, with another increase largely expected by year-end.
The European Central Bank has already moved in the opposite direction. It raised its three key rates by 25 basis points last Thursday, taking the deposit rate to 2.50%, as the Middle East conflict drove renewed inflation pressure.
Dollar gains as Fed decision looms
The dollar has gained more traction in recent sessions as markets increasingly expect the Federal Reserve to resume raising rates.
Traders are looking for the first hike in a potential series of increases, with inflation pressures being reinforced by the surge in energy prices linked to the Middle East conflict.
The latest rise in oil prices has pushed Treasury yields higher and complicated the inflation outlook, particularly for economies that rely heavily on energy imports.
"When the Fed tightens, it normally raises rates at sequential meetings, which is our current expectation despite the proximity of the October policy meeting to the midterm elections," analysts at ANZ said in a note.
Yen falls as BOJ hike bets remain firm
The yen weakened to around 155.34 per dollar, after touching a one-week low of 155.43 in Asian trading.
Still, the currency remains in the midst of its strongest rally in months, supported by a shift toward more hawkish expectations for Japanese interest rates, coordinated intervention by Japan and the United States, and signs that Japanese investors are bringing overseas funds home.
Markets see about an 80% probability that the BOJ will raise rates on Friday. They are also pricing two 25-basis-point increases by the end of January.
Bank of America analysts said the probability of consecutive increases remains low and would rise materially only if the USD/JPY pair were to reverse its recent decline completely and move back toward levels seen before the intervention.
Won, yuan remain in focus across Asia
The South Korean won was weaker, with the USD/KRW pair rising 0.2% to 1,364.73.
The won has nevertheless strengthened more than 15% against the dollar since the end of June, supported by repatriated capital and profits generated by South Korean chipmakers.
The Chinese yuan remained resilient, with the USD/CNH pair around 6.7104 and USD/CNY near 6.7098.
The yuan’s extended rally has lost momentum around the 6.71 level, but it has held onto its gains despite the widening gap between China’s relatively low interest rates and yields elsewhere.
Other currencies were mixed. The USD/SGD pair rose 0.1% to 1.2732, while USD/INR fell 0.1% to 95.986. The USD/MYR pair dropped sharply to 4.0446, while USD/IDR edged higher to 17,707.7.
With the Fed decision due Wednesday and the BOJ meeting on Friday, the dollar-yen relationship is likely to remain central to Asian FX markets.

Germany’s policy-sensitive two-year Schatz yield anchored at 3.25%, near its highest level in three years, reflecting persistent market pricing for an extended cycle of central bank restrictiveness.
Meanwhile, benchmark 10-year German Bund yields lingered at 3.544%, their highest levels since 2011. In contrast, longer-dated paper saw a modest reprise after days of aggressive selling. Yields on ultra-long German paper, the 30-year note, eased from 15-year highs to trade around 3.897%.
France’s 30-year yield similarly pulled back from its highest levels since 2002, offering temporary relief to long-end duration curves that track long-term inflation, economic growth, and structural fiscal deficit expectations.
All eyes on Washington as Fed rate hike looms
The consolidation across European sovereign curves comes as transatlantic attention shifts squarely to the Federal Open Market Committee’s policy announcement later in the day.
Financial markets have priced in roughly a 92% probability that Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh and the FOMC will raise borrowing costs by 25 basis points - marking the U.S. central bank’s first interest rate hike since mid-2023.
The repricing follows the European Central Bank’s decision last week to raise its benchmark deposit facility rate to 2.50%.
Fixed-income desks are focused on Chair Warsh’s post-meeting press conference to parse whether the Fed views the quarter-point move as a standalone, insurance recalibration against energy market volatility or the opening salvo of a broader tightening cycle to tame persistent cost-push inflation.
Energy shock and central bank triad keep yields elevated
Despite the daily pullback in long-dated yields, European debt bourses remain anchored by an elevated risk premium as triple-digit crude oil continues to threaten corporate and consumer inflation expectations.
With Brent crude holding firm past $113 a barrel following strikes on Saudi pipeline infrastructure and Red Sea shipping bottlenecks, money markets show traders are pricing in high odds of another quarter-point ECB rate hike before year-end, alongside further tightening from the Bank of Japan on Friday.

title: UK inflation accelerates to 3.1% in August on sharp rise in fuel prices
full_text:
U.S. stocks end in the red a day ahead of Fed rate decision as yields, oil surge
Investing.com -- British consumer price inflation rose to 3.1% in the 12 months to August from 2.9% in July, matching forecasts and adding to debate over the outlook for Bank of England interest rates as higher fuel costs pushed inflation further above the central bank’s projections, the Office for National Statistics said on Wednesday.
The reading was the highest since December 2025. On a monthly basis, prices rose 0.5% in August, also in line with forecasts, compared with a 0.3% increase a year earlier.
Transport prices rose 4.6% in the year to August, accelerating from 3.6% in July, while prices rose 1.5% in the month, compared with a 0.4% increase a year earlier.
The average price of petrol rose 9.1 pence per litre between July and August, compared with a 0.3 pence increase a year earlier, taking the average to 161.3 pence per litre, the highest since November 2022.
Diesel prices rose 14.2 pence per litre, versus a 0.8 pence increase a year earlier, reaching 181.8 pence per litre. Motor fuel prices rose 23.0% in the year to August, up from 15.5% in July.
Air fares rose 6.2% between July and August, driven by long-haul routes, while housing and household services prices rose 4.9% in the year to August, up from 4.6% in July.
Core CPI, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, held at 2.6%. The CPI all-goods index rose 2.7% in the year to August, up from 2.2% in July and its highest rate since September 2025, while the CPI all-services index remained at 3.4%. Food and non-alcoholic beverage inflation was unchanged at 1.3%.
Deutsche Bank Chief UK Economist Sanjay Raja said headline inflation was 0.25 percentage points above the Bank of England’s forecast, while services inflation was 20 basis points above projections.
Raja said private rents rose 0.49% in the month, their biggest increase since November 2024. Catering prices rose 0.45%, their highest increase since February, while health services prices rose 0.4%. He said the figures indicated that "cost of living pressures is intensifying."
Deutsche Bank expects inflation to approach 4% around the turn of the year, partly due to an expected rise of more than 20% in the Ofgem energy price cap in January. Raja said "the likelihood of rate hikes have strengthened of late."
ING Developed Markets Economist James Smith said there was "nothing in the latest data that screams a need to hike interest rates," noting that the energy shock had not spread to other categories and that food inflation fell to 1.1% year-on-year in August.
ING expects the Bank of England to keep rates on hold into 2027, with inflation peaking at around 3.7% early next year, assuming the household energy cap rises by about 25% in January.
Smith said any rate hike in November would be driven by sustained high energy prices rather than Wednesday’s data.
The Consumer Prices Index including owner occupiers’ housing costs (CPIH) rose 3.3% in the year to August, up from 3.1% in July. Core CPIH held at 2.9%.
Retail Prices Index inflation was 3.4% in the year to August.
